books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Minority report, Senate Select Committee to Investigate the Causes of the Removal of the Negroes from the Southern States to the Northern States, Senate Report 693 (1880)

stimulus.text:
“In the spring of 1879, thousands of colored people, unable longer to endure the intolerable hardships, injustice, and suffering inflicted upon them by a class of Democrats in the South, had, in utter despair, fled panic-stricken from their homes and sought protection among strangers in a strange land. Homeless, penniless, and in rags, these poor people were thronging the wharves of Saint Louis, crowding the steamers on the Mississippi River, and in pitiable destitution throwing themselves upon the charity of Kansas.”

—Minority report, Senate Select Committee to Investigate the Causes of the Removal of the Negroes from the Southern States to the Northern States, 1880
stimulus.source_note: Minority report of the Senate Select Committee investigating the Negro Exodus, Senate Report 693, 46th Congress, 2nd Session (1880). Public domain (congressional report; text verified against the National Archives, “Exodus to Kansas,” Prologue, Summer 2008).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Exodus of 1879 is best understood as evidence that

options.text: Black Southerners sought freedom on their own when federal protection failed.
the Compromise of 1877 had improved life for Black Southerners.
options.misconception: The migration came because life got worse after 1877, not better.

options.text: Northern states welcomed Black migrants with open arms.
options.misconception: Background: the migrants arrived homeless and in rags, dependent on charity; Kansas was a refuge, not a feast.

options.text: sharecropping had made most Black families wealthy enough to move.
options.misconception: Background: sharecropping kept families in debt; the migrants fled poverty, not from plenty.

rationales.A: No law sent them west and no army escorted them. When the troops left and the Redeemers took over, thousands of Black families packed what they owned and walked toward Kansas. It was self-help on a mass scale, the vote with their feet.
rationales.B: The migration came because life got worse after 1877, not better.
rationales.C: Background: the migrants arrived homeless and in rags, dependent on charity; Kansas was a refuge, not a feast.
rationales.D: Background: sharecropping kept families in debt; the migrants fled poverty, not from plenty.
rationales.general:
1. The report describes thousands moving on their own, crowding steamers and wharves.
2. Background: the Compromise of 1877 had removed the troops that once guarded Black rights.
3. With no federal protection left, the migrants protected themselves by leaving.
4. Their movement was a political act: a people choosing the road over a home that had turned against them.
Remember: migration is an argument made with feet, and the Exodusters were answering the failure of Reconstruction.
